scenes.narration: This is Tokio Kamiya, with a dispatch from Shimonoseki, 1865. Eighty men stand ready to march against an entire domain. Within three months, they will have taken it. How does one young rebel pull that off?

scenes.narration: I'm Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent. My grandfather's brass pocket watch carries me to any moment in Japan's past, one day at a time. I can watch and speak, but I can never change a thing. Today I walk the castle town of Hagi, 1857, where the record says Takasugi Shinsaku, born in 1839, is the only son and heir of a household of two hundred koku, a smallpox survivor and a restless, clever young man. His father expects a quiet career. Then, still in his teens, the boy walks into a cramped little schoolhouse.

No text visible anywhere.

scenes.narration: Inside, I find Yoshida Shoin, a thin, burning scholar who teaches that loyalty to Japan matters more than loyalty to any single lord. Poor foot soldiers sit beside the sons of retainers. I watch Shinsaku, proud and sharp-tongued, find his match in a fellow student, Kusaka Genzui, and the two become rivals who push each other higher. Shoin prizes them both. Within two years, I know, the school will be gone. But Shinsaku never stops hearing his teacher's voice.

Warm light from a traditional paper andon lantern only (no candles, no candlesticks, no Western lamps), dust in the air, intimate and intense atmosphere. No text, no writing, no calligraphy on walls, scrolls or notebooks — all paper is blank.

scenes.narration: I cannot follow what comes next, so I read the record. In late 1858, Shoin's radical plotting lands him in his own domain's prison. The next year, the shogunate summons him to Edo, and in late 1859 he is executed in the Ansei Purge. He is twenty-nine. Shinsaku, barely twenty, visited him in his Edo cell, but was ordered home only days before the end. Shoin had preached that Japan would be saved not by lords, but by ordinary people rising up. The shogunate answered with a blade. Where others saw an ending, Shinsaku saw an order.

Somber, muted palette, cold light, the moment before the end. No text visible.

scenes.narration: On another day, the watch sets me on a Shanghai quay in 1862, where Shinsaku has come aboard a shogunate ship sent by his domain. I watch what shakes him. Chinese laborers are shoved aside by European soldiers, and Western officials rule the foreign settlements as if they own them. Nearby, the great Taiping rebellion is tearing the Qing empire apart. His diary will say that Japan could suffer the same fate. He will come home convinced of one thing: the shogunate will not save Japan. Something new will have to.

scenes.narration: Back in Japan, his anger finds a target. At the end of January 1863, I crouch in the dark at Gotenyama, on the edge of Edo, where the British legation is under construction. Shinsaku and a band of young Choshu radicals, including a young Ito Hirobumi, slip in and burn it to the ground. I cannot stop them. The culprits are never publicly punished. Weeks later, the record says, they move Shoin's remains to an honored new grave. Shinsaku, twenty-three, has learned something dangerous: that reckless boldness can work.

scenes.narration: On another day, I stand on a hill above the Shimonoseki Strait. In June 1863, Choshu fired on foreign ships passing through, answering the Emperor's call to expel the barbarians. Within weeks, I watch American and French warships strike back, sinking Choshu's vessels and silencing its shore batteries. The samurai who defend the coast, proud hereditary warriors with swords and old cannon, are routed. Takasugi has shaved his head that spring and withdrawn from public life, but now his lord summons him. I think he draws the lesson Shanghai had hinted at: the samurai class, alone, cannot defend Japan.

Grim, chaotic aftermath of defeat. No text visible.

scenes.narration: His lord puts him in charge of defending Shimonoseki, and Takasugi proposes something radical. That summer, he founds the Kiheitai, the irregular corps. On a drill ground I see him recruit by skill and courage, not by birth. Samurai stand beside farmers and townsmen, though samurai still hold many of the command posts, and similar units follow, one of sumo wrestlers. They drill with Western rifles, a few hundred men at first. To the old guard, it is an insult. To Takasugi, it is the only army that can save Choshu.

scenes.narration: Then everything collapses. In August 1864, I read, Choshu's attempt to seize the imperial court in Kyoto fails in disaster, and the shogunate brands Choshu a rebel domain. Weeks later, a fleet of four foreign nations bombards Shimonoseki again, and I watch the smoke rise over the strait. Released from confinement, Takasugi is sent to negotiate the peace. A British interpreter wrote that he came aboard as proud as Lucifer, and tradition says he refused to surrender an inch of Japanese land. Meanwhile, conservatives at home, desperate to appease the shogunate, seize power.

He stares back with proud, unyielding calm while the officers lean toward him; through the open stern windows the smoking ruins of coastal forts are visible. scenes.narration: I come to the Shimonoseki waterfront in the winter of 1864, posing as a travelling merchant. The conservatives have arrested reformers and ordered the Kiheitai disbanded. Takasugi fled to Fukuoka, a hunted man, and in December slipped back to Shimonoseki by boat. An old fisherman told me that the Kiheitai's own commanders, fearing the domain's army, hesitated to follow him. Only a handful would join. Takasugi is left with a choice: run to safety, or attempt something no one in Choshu believes possible. He is twenty-five, hunted, and out of allies.

scenes.narration: On the night of January 12th, 1865, I stand in the frozen courtyard of Kozan-ji temple in Shimonoseki. Takasugi faces about eighty men: Ito Hirobumi's wrestlers, and Ishikawa Kogoro's ranger corps. Against them stands the domain's army of thousands. To the exiled court nobles sheltering at the temple, he declares that he will now show them what a man of Choshu can do. Then he turns and marches. Eighty men, with no permission from their lord and no guarantee of victory, set out to take back their own domain. I cannot stop them.

scenes.narration: I get one afternoon on the Mitajiri quay; the record gives the rest. The rebels seize the domain's office in Shimonoseki, then raid its naval station here and capture its warships. Villagers shelter and supply them. The hesitant Kiheitai commanders finally join. In February 1865, they defeat the domain army in a string of battles in the hills of central Choshu, with modern rifles against a larger old-style force. By March, the reformists control Choshu. A tiny band, led by a man of twenty-five, has overturned the government of one of Japan's largest domains.

scenes.narration: I did not see the year that follows, so I read it. With Choshu in reformist hands, the domain rebuilds itself around Western arms, buying modern rifles and a steamship through the British merchant Thomas Glover. New units drill with them, commoners and samurai side by side. Even Choshu's old enemy Satsuma quietly helps, and by early 1866 the two domains form a secret alliance. Takasugi, now twenty-six, will soon command Choshu's small navy. Everyone knows the shogunate will come. The domain has months, not years. And I know that Takasugi himself has even less time than he knows.

scenes.narration: On another day, in the summer of 1866, I watch from a hill above Oshima. The shogunate has sent its armies to crush Choshu, on four fronts at once, against a fraction of the force. When shogunate troops seize the island, I watch Takasugi take the Heiin Maru, a small steamship he has just bought, and in a night attack sail in among the shogunate's anchored warships, firing as he goes. It is Choshu's first counterblow, and the record says the island is retaken within days. A war everyone expects Choshu to lose has begun to turn.

scenes.narration: I read the dispatches for the other fronts. Across the fronts, the shogunate's army falters. Choshu's mixed troops with modern rifles beat the larger feudal forces again and again, and Takasugi leads the fight across the strait toward Kokura. Then, in late August, the shogun Tokugawa Iemochi dies in Osaka Castle. The shogunate's commander in Kyushu slips away, and its abandoned ally Kokura sets fire to its own castle and retreats. The war fizzles into a humiliating truce. A single domain has beaten the shogunate's armies. I think the Tokugawa aura of invincibility is gone.

scenes.narration: Takasugi has no time to celebrate. That autumn, he begins coughing blood. My last stop is Shimonoseki, spring 1867, outside a small house. He has retired here, thin and feverish, nursed by the Buddhist nun and poet Nomura Boto, who once hid him in Fukuoka. I do not go in. Tradition says he wrote the first half of a poem: to make this dull world interesting. Boto is said to have finished it, by adding that it was a matter of the heart. On the 17th of May, 1867, Takasugi Shinsaku dies of tuberculosis. He is twenty-seven.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Less than six months later, in November 1867, the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, handed his power back to the Emperor. The system that had ruled Japan for over two and a half centuries was finished. Choshu's soldiers, trained in the model Takasugi had built, marched with the imperial forces in the war that followed. He did not live to see any of it. I think the Japan we know today begins there: the age of the shoguns was over.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. The men around Takasugi went on to build modern Japan. Ito Hirobumi became its first prime minister. Yamagata Aritomo, who later led the Kiheitai, built the modern army. But the corps itself met a bitter end. When Choshu disbanded it, some of its veterans rebelled, and in 1870 they were crushed. The revolution consumed its own army. Then, in 1873, Yamagata helped introduce national conscription, drawing soldiers from every class. It was the same principle the Kiheitai had tested. I think Takasugi's idea outlived his army.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. It is easy to inflate the legend, and I try not to. The Kiheitai was never simply an army of peasants. It was a mix, and many of its leaders were lower samurai. Takasugi himself was a samurai who fought for Choshu, not for equality. And he did not topple the shogunate alone: Satsuma, and go-betweens like Sakamoto Ryoma, mattered just as much. I think his true achievement was proving that a motivated, mixed force with modern weapons could beat the shogunate. After that, everyone believed it could be done.

scenes.narration: Takasugi lived as if he knew his time was short, and he spent it trying to make a dull world interesting. History rarely rewards that kind of impatience, yet it was his impatience that cracked open a shogunate. He asked who could defend Japan, and he answered with ordinary men and modern guns. I would like to meet more people like him, with you. If you want to come along, you know where to find us. The watch is ticking. Until the next report. Tokio Kamiya, reporting.
